title: Settle on the mat
note:
Cover for an activity not built yet; the worklist alt text is the brief. The worklist says 'mat'; the recurring prop across the whole library is the cool-grey dog bed, so this uses the bed rather than introducing a second piece of furniture that means the same thing.

The distinguisher is the SLEEP. Every other picture in the set that has Lucy settled has her in a sphinx down with her head up and her eyes open, watching something. This one is flat on her side with her eyes shut, which is the only place in the library that pose appears, and it is what separates the cover from door-greet-06-seated — a dog settled between two seated people with her head up. One person here, not two, and she is asleep rather than watching.

Interior, so it needs nothing the live brief does not already define.
scene: Interior living space, the pale lavender wall and desaturated oak floor, one baseboard line. FOUR THINGS ONLY: a plain armchair in muted slate-blue, Lucy's cool-grey dog bed, the wall and the floor — no side table, no rug, no plant, no framed picture, no lamp, no door, no doormat. Lucy is ASLEEP on the bed — a proper mattress with real thickness, a padded slab about a hand deep with a soft raised edge, not a flat mat — and she is lying FLAT ON HER SIDE, not in an upright sphinx down: her shoulder and hip are both down on the mattress, her legs are extended loosely out to one side, her head is resting flat on the bed rather than held up, and HER EYES ARE CLOSED. She is deeply and obviously asleep. The handler sits quietly in the armchair a little way off, settled back and at ease, hands resting in her lap, reading or simply looking ahead — she is NOT looking at Lucy, not reaching toward her and not touching her. Nothing is happening: this is a picture of a dog who has switched off in company. No leash, no treat. HOW BIG THE PAIR IS DRAWN: draw them SMALLER than the composition wants, grouped close together near the middle rather than spread across the frame. The top of the highest head sits about a QUARTER of the way down from the top edge and no higher; the lowest thing that matters no lower than three quarters of the way down. Above every head leave a clear band of empty lavender wall at least a fifth of the picture height with nothing in it, and below them clear empty floor. Left and right, nothing that matters enters the outer eighth of the width. The app crops this two ways at once — a wide Today band keeping only the middle strip of the HEIGHT, and a centred square keeping only the middle three-quarters of the WIDTH — so a head near the top edge is decapitated on the app largest surface. Empty wall above them is better than a sliced head.
mustBeTrue: Lucy is lying flat on her side with her shoulder and hip down, her legs extended, her head resting on the bed and her eyes closed — asleep rather than in an upright sphinx down with her head up — the handler is seated a little way off and is not looking at her, touching her or reaching toward her, and the top of her head sits about a quarter of the way down the frame with clear wall above it and nothing that matters in the top fifth, the bottom quarter or the outer eighth of either side.
